columns.heading: What Paid Off
columns.body: In a completed-week review, the biggest fantasy edge usually came from backing players with believable advancement paths and repeatable scoring traits rather than chasing pure volatility. Builds anchored by stable servers, efficient match winners, and players who avoided early-round danger generally gave themselves the best chance to compound points across the week.
bullets: Advancement equity again proved more valuable than one-match upside.
Bonus Ball discipline typically rewarded the steadiest path, not the flashiest pick.
Serve-driven scoring profiles remained useful because aces and cleaner wins stack quickly.
Balanced builds usually outperformed lineups that forced too many fragile upside bets.

columns.heading: What Likely Missed
columns.body: The most common misses in a finished week usually come from overrating name value, underestimating bracket resistance, or doubling down on volatility with the Bonus Ball. Cheap players without a realistic route still burn roster spots, and premium salaries become difficult to justify when they need multiple tight wins just to reach the rounds that matter.
bullets: Crowded sections often turned popular picks into weak fantasy investments.
False value remained a trap when salary relief came with a likely early exit.
Bonus Ball misses were most damaging when attached to unstable paths.
Lineups built around too many coin-flip matches usually lacked staying power.

cards.title: What Matters Most After The Week Ends
paragraphs: ATP Fantasy still rewards the same core structure: 100 credits, six starters, two alternates, and one Bonus Ball player scoring double. In a results edition, the key takeaway is not just who won matches, but which roster-building ideas actually translated into usable fantasy scoring over a full week.

Because the primary ATP results, rankings, and news packets were unavailable in this cycle, this edition stays intentionally conservative on player-specific outcomes. The safest takeaway is structural: fantasy success usually came from combining advancement equity with portable scoring traits such as ace production, hold stability, and the ability to finish matches efficiently. Those are the lessons worth carrying into the next slate.
cards.subtitle: Results Edition Themes
bullets: Completed weeks usually reward path quality more than pre-slate hype.
Bonus Ball outcomes often decide whether a good lineup becomes a great one.
Value matters most when it survives long enough to compound points.
Misses often trace back to volatility in crowded draw pockets.

items.body: Start with players who can realistically string together multiple wins, then use value around them. The strongest lineups usually did not need repeated upsets to stay live.
Players who paired advancement with ace volume or efficient straight-set wins remained the most reliable fantasy engines over the course of the week.
Reading route quality correctly still mattered more than reacting to reputation alone. Cleaner sections generally produced the most useful fantasy totals.
When a popular option entered the week with a dangerous lane or several likely long matches, that risk often showed up in the final fantasy returns.

cards.title: Who Usually Outperformed In A Week Like This

items.body: Expensive players tended to justify salary when their path let them reach the later rounds without burning too much scoring equity in early danger spots.
The best mid-range plays were typically the ones with a realistic route to two or more wins plus enough serve or return quality to keep scoring even in tighter matches.
Players who benefited from a softer section or a more manageable early sequence often delivered better fantasy value than similarly priced peers in tougher lanes.
The multiplier usually worked best on the player with the clearest path to multiple wins and the most repeatable scoring profile.
An aggressive Bonus Ball can still succeed when it lands on a player with genuine route equity and enough ace or straight-set upside to separate.
The weakest multiplier outcomes generally came from volatile picks in contested sections, especially when they needed several close wins just to stay alive.
If two Bonus Ball candidates look close, lean toward the one less dependent on tiebreaks, long matches, or upset-heavy sequencing.
Useful salary relief usually came from players priced below the top tier who still had a believable route to bank at least one or two wins.
Lower-cost options outperformed when the bracket reduced early obstacles and let their serve or baseline stability translate into immediate points.
The most effective alternates were not just cheap placeholders; they were players with real advancement equity if the main build needed coverage.
Serve-led players remained attractive value shapes because ace totals and hold-based stability can produce fantasy utility even before a deep run develops.
Overexposure to heavily contested sections usually limited lineup ceilings because strong names eliminated each other before fantasy totals could fully build.
Cheap players with difficult openers still hurt lineups, especially when managers treated salary relief as enough reason to roster them.
Popular players were still vulnerable fantasy fades when their route offered little margin for error relative to price.
Doubling a volatile player in a dangerous lane remained one of the fastest ways to turn an otherwise solid roster into a losing week.
